Description: Shebang: the first line of a script, telling the system to run it with Bash
Ends the script; its exit code tells whether it worked (0) or failed (anything else)
Runs the command inside the parentheses and uses its output (command substitution)
Runs the command in a subshell, a child process separate from the main script
Declares a variable and assigns it some text (no spaces around the =)
Reads a variable's value; the braces mark where the name ends when it's stuck to other text
Declares variables with attributes, for example making them integers
Does arithmetic on variables
Holds the name of the script as it was called from the terminal
The first, second (and so on) argument passed on the command line
Holds the number of arguments passed on the command line
Holds all the arguments passed on the command line in a single variable
Processes the options a script receives (-m, -h...) one at a time; usually used inside a while loop
Holds the value that comes with the option getopts is currently processing
Runs a block if the condition is true and another one (else) if it isn't; closed with fi
Example: if [ $n -eq 1 ]; then echo "one"; else echo "other"; fi

Description: Compares a variable against several patterns and runs the block that matches; closed with esac
Example: case $arg in m) echo "option m";; esac

Description: Loops over a list of items one by one, running a block of code for each
Example: for i in $(seq 1 5); do echo $i; done

Description: Repeats a block of code while a condition is true
Generates a sequence of numbers within a range, handy for loops
Brace expansion: generates a sequence of values (here 0000 to 9999), useful as a counter in loops
Example: for i in {0000..9999}; do echo $i; done

Description: Defines a custom function that groups several commands under one name
Catches a signal (like Ctrl+C) and runs a function instead of stopping the script right away
Waits for one or more background processes to finish before continuing
Runs a command and kills it if it takes longer than the given time
Creates a temporary file with a unique name, avoiding clashes with other files
Controls the terminal, for example hiding or showing the cursor
Special Bash path that opens a TCP connection to an IP and port as if it were a file, no netcat needed
Sends requests to a URL from the terminal (HTTP, HTTPS, etc.) and shows the response
Shows a file like cat, but with syntax highlighting and line numbers
Formats minified JavaScript or JSON so it's readable (line breaks and indentation)
